metadata.title: Half Cross stitch in needlepoint / canvaswork embroidery | Needlepoint stitches video tutorial
metadata.description:
How to stitch half cross stitch in needlepoint. Know the differences between this stitch and Basketweave stitch & Tent stitch! See Basketweave stitch: https://youtu.be/f7Ijx9-znaE 
and Tent stitch: https://youtu.be/Bp3Wa9FBYtM
This is just one in an extensive playlist exploring this popular hand embroidery technique and demonstrating many needlepoint stitches. See all 29 videos in the playlist here: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLC2TZFIW8ZoPqCobgEK91t45YFnJlIIVV

Presented by Sarah Homfray, a graduate of The Royal School of Needlework 3-year apprenticeship and a professional hand embroiderer and  tutor.

Please Like, Share and Subscribe to keep these videos coming! 

Sign up for my monthly e-mail Newsletter: https://www.sarahhomfray.com/newsletter.html

Visit https://www.sarahhomfray.com for your hand embroidery supplies.
Hand embroidery for beginners and experts!
#SarahHomfrayEmbroidery #SarahHomfrayStitchLibrary #SarahHomfrayNeedlepoint

summary.brief: The instructor demonstrates how to execute a half‑cross stitch on needlepoint using green thread.
summary.detailed: After a short title slide and music, a woman in a white T‑shirt sits beside an embroidery hoop that holds a canvas with a green‑thread design. She explains that the half‑cross stitch looks identical on the front to other stitches but differs on the back, using less thread and producing a flatter back side. Threading a needle with green yarn, she pushes the needle up from underneath the canvas at the intersection of two warp and weft threads, forming a small diagonal forward stitch, then drives the needle down into the next hole that shares a corner with the previous stitch. She repeats this forward motion from left to right, showing that each stitch appears as a vertical line on the back. She advises always inserting the needle into a hole that already contains thread to avoid splitting the yarn and highlights the stitch’s economy of thread, making it suitable for budget projects or when a thin back is desired. After completing a row, she demonstrates that changing direction (working reverse) would create a ten‑stitch instead of a half‑cross stitch, so she emphasizes keeping the needle on the same side and moving in the same direction when starting the next row. The tutorial concludes with an end‑card advertising embroidery products.

action.detailed: Thread a needle with green yarn, push it up through a hole at a canvas intersection, pull it through, drive the needle down into the adjacent hole to form a diagonal forward stitch, and repeat the motion across the fabric to create the half‑cross stitch pattern.
action.actor: the female instructor in a white T‑shirt

summary.brief: A woman demonstrates how to work a half‑cross stitch on a needlepoint canvas and later adds beads to a needle‑and‑thread pattern.
summary.detailed: The video opens with the presenter showing the appearance of a half‑cross stitch on the front of a needlepoint canvas. She pulls the needle up from beneath the fabric, inserts it into the lower hole at an intersection of the canvas threads, and brings the thread up through the opposite hole to form a small diagonal stitch on the front. She repeats this forward motion across the row, keeping the needle in holes that already contain thread to avoid splitting the yarn, and explains that each forward stitch produces a vertical stitch on the back, uses less thread and keeps the back flatter. After completing a row she demonstrates how to finish the end, turn the work, and either continue on the same side with the same thread or start a new thread while maintaining the same direction. A close‑up shows her thumb holding green thread as the needle moves. The tutorial then shifts to a segment where she threads a needle, with the right side of the split screen zooming in on the threading process while she narrates. Finally, she switches to placing small beads on a needle and forming a horizontal bead line on a board, again using green thread as a guide. The segment ends with a brief promotional screen displaying the website for embroidery supplies.

action.detailed: Insert the needle from underneath the canvas into a lower hole at each thread intersection, pull the thread up through the opposite hole to create a diagonal stitch on the front and a vertical stitch on the back, and repeat the forward motion across the row while keeping the needle in already‑threaded holes to avoid splitting the thread.

summary.brief: The instructor demonstrates how to make a half‑cross stitch in needlepoint.
summary.detailed: The video begins with the instructor seated beside an embroidery hoop, holding a needle threaded with green yarn. She explains that a half‑cross stitch looks the same as a regular cross stitch on the front but forms a short vertical stitch on the back, using less thread and keeping the back flat. Starting at a point on the canvas, she pushes the needle under the fabric and brings it up through a diagonal hole, creating a small diagonal stitch across the intersection of the canvas threads. She repeats this forward‑direction stitch, always entering a hole that already contains thread so the needle does not split the yarn. On the reverse side each stitch appears as a vertical line, conserving yarn and preventing bulk. She shows the end of a row and warns that stitching back in the opposite direction would produce a tent stitch rather than a half‑cross stitch, so the next stitch must start on the same side and continue in the same direction. The close‑up view alternates between the needle, the grid of the canvas, and the growing stitch pattern as she works through the segment.

action.detailed: Insert the needle through the canvas, pull the thread to form a diagonal stitch across each intersecting hole, and repeat the forward‑direction stitches so the front shows a half‑cross stitch while the back shows a short vertical stitch, always entering holes that already contain thread to conserve yarn and keep the back flat.

summary.brief: The presenter demonstrates how to make a half‑cross stitch on an embroidery canvas.
summary.detailed: At the start of the segment the instructor, wearing a white shirt and a small microphone, holds a needle threaded with green yarn. The camera alternates between close‑ups of her thumb and the needle and a wider view of the canvas. She inserts the needle under the warp threads, pulls it up through the next hole to create a small diagonal stitch across the intersection, then drives the needle down into the adjacent hole that already contains thread, taking care not to split the existing thread. She repeats this forward motion across the row, showing the front of the work where the stitches look like normal cross stitches and then turning the canvas over to reveal a short vertical stitch on the back, illustrating the reduced thread usage and flatter back. After completing the row she gestures to the end of the stitch, explains that the next row must start from the same side and in the same direction, and demonstrates beginning the next row while continuing to point to the canvas. Throughout the segment she periodically zooms in on the needle and thread to highlight the stitching process.

action.detailed: Insert the needle under the canvas threads, pull it up through the next hole to form a diagonal stitch, then drive the needle down into the adjacent hole that already holds thread without splitting it, pull up again, and repeat this forward motion across the row while checking both the front and back sides of the work.

summary.brief: The presenter demonstrates how to work a half‑cross stitch on a needlepoint canvas.
summary.detailed: The woman sits in front of a needlepoint canvas showing a black‑and‑white grid with two rows of green yarn in the centre. She introduces the half‑cross stitch, explaining that it looks like a small diagonal stitch on the front while producing a vertical stitch on the back. She shows the needle starting from the back of the canvas, pulling it up through a diagonal intersection of the warp and weft threads, then pushing it down into the next hole that shares a thread with the previous row. She repeats this forward motion, working from left to right, creating a short line of half‑cross stitches and pointing out the vertical back‑side stitch. She notes that this stitch uses less thread and gives a flatter back than other stitches, and warns that stitching in the opposite direction would produce a different stitch (tent stitch). Finally she mentions that each new row must start from the same side and be worked in the same direction to keep the half‑cross stitch consistent.

action.detailed: Insert the needle from the back of the canvas, pull it up through a diagonal intersection, push it down into the adjacent hole that shares a thread, and repeat the motion to form a line of half‑cross stitches.

summary.brief: The instructor demonstrates half‑cross stitching on a canvas, working forward across a row and then shows a variant stitch pattern.

She repeats this motion, moving left‑to‑right, so each front‑side stitch appears as a forward half‑cross while the back side shows a straight vertical stitch. She notes that this method uses less thread and gives a flatter back. After completing the row, she explains how to start the next row by beginning on the same side and continuing in the same direction, or by starting a new thread if the previous one is finished. She then demonstrates another stitch pattern that involves three consecutive down‑strokes followed by two up‑strokes, continuing to work on the same canvas as shown in the close‑up on the right.

summary.brief: The instructor demonstrates the half‑cross stitch, showing the diagonal front stitch and the vertical back stitch while explaining its thread‑saving, flatter‑back advantages.
summary.detailed: Seated at her light‑colored embroidery board, the woman in a white t‑shirt threads a needle with green yarn and inserts it from the back of the canvas. She pulls the needle up through an intersection to create a small forward‑diagonal stitch on the front, then drives the needle down into the adjacent hole, producing a straight vertical stitch on the back. She repeats this forward‑down sequence across the row, all the while commenting that the half‑cross stitch uses less thread, leaves a flatter surface on the back of the work, and may require a slightly thicker or doubled thread for full coverage. The background shows a white wall with a green curtain and a wooden stand holding the canvas.

summary.brief: The presenter finishes a row of half‑cross stitches, shows why stitching backward gives a different stitch, and explains how to start the next row correctly.
summary.detailed: Seated in a wooden chair in front of her embroidery hoop, the woman in a beige top and a pendant with a diamond works the green thread on the canvas against a turquoise curtain. She brings the needle up through the final hole of the current row, pulls the thread tight and makes the last diagonal half‑cross stitch to finish the row. She then turns the needle and stitches leftward, demonstrating that this backward motion produces a back stitch (a ten‑stitch) rather than another half‑cross. While the close‑up on the right follows the needle and thread, she explains that the next row must be started on the same side and worked forward again, either by pulling the existing thread underneath or by beginning a new thread, to maintain the half‑cross pattern.

action.detailed: Insert the needle into the last hole of the canvas, pull the green thread through to complete the final half‑cross stitch, then reverse direction to demonstrate a back stitch and explain that the next row should be started on the same side and worked forward again.

She talks and gestures, and a picture‑in‑picture inset shows a close‑up of her deep‑red hands guiding a metal needle with a purple handle through the tiny woven holes of the loom’s fabric, drawing the yarn through each hole and onto the loop. She repeats this motion while continuing her verbal explanation.

action.detailed: Insert the needle into a loom hole, draw the yarn through the hole with the needle, guide the yarn onto the loop on the peg, and repeat the process for successive holes.
